Signal to Signature

One workbench for the whole radio-frequency story of a lightweight structure. Start from a material — the flagship is MXene-coated basswood — and get, instantly: the loss, mass and launch cost of a waveguide built from it; the gain, beamwidth and efficiency of a horn antenna; the reflection loss of a radar-absorbing coating straight from your measured ε/μ; and the radar cross section of a real 3-D CAD model you upload, part by part — including how much smaller a coating makes it look to a radar. Inverse design and parametric sweeps search the space for you, and every analytical answer can be checked against a genuine openEMS full-wave FDTD solve, always plotted together (dashed = model, solid = full-wave) so the agreement is visible rather than promised.

Analytical + openEMS FDTD · X · Ku · K waveguide bands, 0.5–110 GHz radar · STEP/STL import · measured ε/μ · weight & launch-cost aware

Created by Huzaifa Taha Rangwala (UC Berkeley) · Space Materials Lab, Khalifa University · To download or for more information, contact huzaifataha54@berkeley.edu

Click any card for what it means.

Loss · per metre
–
Signal lost per metre travelling down the guide (mid-band). Lower is better — copper is about 0.11 dB/m.
Transmitted · over run
–
How much signal reaches the far end over the chosen run length (S21). 0 dB = nothing lost; more negative = more lost.
Power through · over run
–
Fraction of the input power that arrives at the far end over the run length. 100% = perfect, 50% = half lost.
Best frequency
–
The frequency in this band with the lowest loss — where the guide performs best.
Weight · full run
–
Mass of the four waveguide walls for the chosen run length. Lighter = cheaper to launch.
Delivered cost · run
–
Material cost plus launch cost (mass × $/kg-to-orbit) for the run length.
Break-even launch cost
–
The launch cost above which this material is cheaper to deliver to orbit than copper. Real launch is ~$7,000/kg.
Coating ÷ skin depth
–
Coating thickness compared with the skin depth. It must exceed about 3× the skin depth to reflect like solid metal.
Loss tangent · tan δ
–
Effective loss tangent tan δ = σ_eff/(ωε₀εr′), combining conduction and dielectric loss (εr″). A conductor like MXene sits ≫1; a good low-loss dielectric is ≪1. Set εr″ in the Materials tab to add dielectric loss.
Penetration depth · Dp
–
How far the field reaches into the wall before dropping to 1/e (Eq. S2, Elkaffas et al.). For a good conductor it equals the skin depth; the coating should be several times thicker than this.
Dominant loss mechanism
–
Which of the three absorption channels dominates (Eq. S1): conduction/Joule (½σ|E|²), dielectric (πf ε₀εr″|E|²), or magnetic (πf μ₀μr″|H|²), for a reference incident field. Non-magnetic materials show 0% magnetic; MXene is conduction-dominated.

Attenuation across the band

How fast signal is lost travelling down the guide — lower is better.

Material comparison

MXene-coated basswood vs basswood, copper and aluminum across the factors that matter — higher is better on every axis.

Cost-effectiveness and lightness are computed from the current run (delivered cost & weight per metre); EM performance from the mid-band loss at the ideal (loss-floor) coat count; sustainability is a fixed 0–100 rating the author assigned to the four default materials — it is not computed, and it does not change when you define your own test material, so ignore that axis for a custom material; env-friendly is scored from embodied carbon (CO₂e per kg, lower = greener). Press Show actual numbers for the raw values with units.

          What you're looking at
          
    
            
  • The 3-D box with the bright green outline is the waveguide itself — the wall material you chose (e.g. basswood) with its inner conductive coating (e.g. MXene) lining the inside. The coating is only microns thick, so it is represented by the inner surface, not drawn to scale.
    • 
            
  • The glowing colour is the electric-field strength |E| (see the colour bar, in V/m): bright/red = strong field, dark = little or no field.
    • 
            
  • The wave is launched at one end (the input port) as the TE₁₀ mode and travels along the guide's long axis (left → right in the view).
    • 
            
  • Any colour outside the green outline is signal leaking through the wall — large for a poor conductor (bare wood, too-thin coating), negligible for a good one (MXene, copper, silver).
    • 
            
  • Guided wave = the travelling signal (transmission). Reflection = a wall placed across the far end so the wave bounces back into a standing-wave pattern (fixed bright/dark bands); a strong, stationary pattern means a near-perfect reflector.
    • 
            
  • In Field view → frequency-domain the picture is a single steady |E| snapshot at the band-centre frequency instead of an animation.
    •

Coating comparison — gain penalty vs solid metal

    
Conductor loss on the horn walls, computed from the full-wave field via the surface-impedance method (the surface-impedance boundary method for finite conductivity). Radiation efficiency = radiated ÷ accepted power.

Every coating is computed from a single full-wave PEC solve via the surface-impedance method (a separate lossy FDTD per coating is invalid here — skin depth ≪ mesh), so one run already covers all of them; the Excel carries a sheet per material. A horn's walls are short and lightly loaded, so even MXene (surface resistance ~7.6× copper) costs only a fraction of a dB — unlike a long waveguide, where wall loss accumulates per metre.

    


    
The antenna solve uses open (PML) boundaries + a near-field-to-far-field transform; gain is validated against the horn's rated figure. Conductor loss for each coating is integrated from the full-wave H-field on the walls.

  


  
  

    
    
Radar cross section · openEMS

    
How detectable is a target by radar — and how much does a coating hide it? A plane wave illuminates the target in openEMS; a near-field-to-far-field box captures the scattered field and returns the radar cross section (RCS). The instant analytical curve (exact Mie series for a sphere [37], physical optics for a plate [38]) is overlaid so you can see the full-wave solve tracks it. Coating a metal target with a lossy absorber (magnetite, carbonyl iron, …) lowers the RCS — the reason radar-absorbing materials exist.


    
Run on openEMS — automated

    
Pick the target and run the full-wave RCS solver. (Requires the local bridge: start openEMS/openems_server.py and open this page at http://localhost:8731.) A coated run also solves the bare metal target for the reduction figure, so it takes about twice as long.

Standard RCS benchmarks

      
The canonical targets the computational-electromagnetics community uses to validate an RCS solver, each with the published reference it is checked against. The sphere is this tool's quantitative headline; the rest are named literature targets. In keeping with the honesty rule, every card states plainly how well a Cartesian-grid FDTD can be expected to do. Click Load to configure the controls above — then press Run RCS on openEMS.

      

        

          
Headline · exact

          
Conducting sphere vs Mie series

          
The #1 code-validation case: a PEC sphere has a closed-form exact backscatter from the Mie series [37] — no measurement uncertainty, isotropic, and it sweeps Rayleigh → resonance → optical (σ → πa²) as ka grows. The tool matches it to ~1 dB in the reliable ka ≈ 1–4 window.

          
        

        

          
Analytic reference

          
Flat plate & corner reflector vs PO

          
A flat plate at broadside gives the physical-optics spike σ = 4πA²/λ² [38]; a 90° dihedral retro-reflects over a wide angle (validated to the PO large-reflector bound, run at 45° incidence). Both are canonical specular/multi-bounce tests.

          
          
        

        

          
Literature target

          
NASA almond (Woo et al. 1993)

          
The standard smooth-target CEM benchmark [42]: length 252 mm, monostatic azimuth sweep at 1.19 and 7 GHz, peak backscatter ≈ −15…−20 dBsm. Honest note: it is a smooth curved body — exactly where MoM/PO shine and a Cartesian FDTD grid staircases — so expect a qualitative shape match at 1.19 GHz (≈1λ) and only approximate levels at 7 GHz (≈5.9λ). Load its mesh with STEP / STL import in the configuration panel above.

Radar range & detectability

      
How far away a radar can detect this target, from the classic radar range equation [43] R = [Pt Gt Gr λ² σ / ((4π)³ Pmin L)]1/4. Detection range scales as σ1/4, so a coating that cuts RCS by Δ dB shrinks the range by 10−Δ/40 — the headline reason radar-absorbing material matters. The target RCS auto-fills from your last solve; every field is editable.

Probability of detection vs range

        
The single-number range above is the point where Pd ≈ 50%. Real detection is probabilistic — this curve shows how the detection chance falls off with range, for the bare target vs the coated one. The gap is how much closer the radar must come once the coating is on.

        

        
First-order free-space estimate (no integration gain, no propagation/atmospheric loss, no clutter). Pd from the North approximation (Swerling 0) or the closed-form Swerling-1 (single-pulse) with the Pfa threshold. It answers "how does this RCS change detectability?", not "will this specific radar detect it" — the σ1/4 scaling and the coating trade are the point.

      

    



    
    

      
      
      
      
    

    

    


    
    

    

    

    
Monostatic RCS vs frequency

    
Monostatic means the transmitter and receiver sit together, so this is the backscatter — the echo that comes straight back at the radar — in dBsm (dB relative to 1 m²) across the frequency band. Lower = harder to detect (stealthier). Dashed green = the analytical reference — the exact Mie series for a sphere, and physical optics for a plate (an asymptotic high-frequency approximation: close near broadside, degrading toward grazing); solid = the openEMS full-wave solve, whose magnitude is mesh-limited so read the shape, not the last decibel.

    

    


    

    
Bistatic RCS — H-plane (f₀)

    
A bistatic cut: the wave comes from one fixed direction while a receiver sweeps around the target (in the x-y plane), showing where the scattered energy actually goes. φ = 0° is straight ahead (forward scatter, usually the biggest lobe). The backscatter direction the radar itself sees is φ = 180° + incidence angle — so it coincides with 180° only at normal incidence (e.g. the dihedral, run at 45°, backscatters near −135°). Dashed = analytical (sphere/plate only), solid = openEMS. Only this x-y CSV carries the co-/cross-polarization split.

    

    


    

    
Bistatic RCS — E-plane (f₀)

    
The same bistatic sweep taken in the x-z plane — the principal cut perpendicular to the one above — the plane that contains the radar's E-field (perpendicular to the H-plane cut above). Comparing the two planes shows how the scattering depends on polarization: for a sphere they differ only slightly, for a flat plate they differ by which edge sets the lobe width. Again 0° = forward, ±180° = backscatter; dashed = analytical, solid = openEMS.

    

    


    

    
Monostatic RCS vs aspect angle (turntable)

    
The classic radar signature: the target sits on a turntable and the radar watches the echo as the viewing angle changes — each point is a separate full openEMS solve at band centre. A flat plate flashes brightly at normal incidence and drops fast off-angle; a sphere is the same from every side; a dihedral corner reflector stays bright over a wide angle range (that is what corner reflectors are for). Dashed = physical-optics reference where one exists.

    

    


    

    
Down-range profile — scattering centers

    
The inverse Fourier transform of the complex backscatter across the band turns the frequency sweep into an echo-vs-range plot — the same trick a real wideband radar uses. Each peak is a scattering center: the front-face specular return sits near 0, and delayed peaks are edges or a creeping wave that crawls around the body before re-radiating. A Hann window is applied; range resolution ≈ c/(2·bandwidth). This needs the Monostatic sim (it supplies the complex data).

    

    

    


    

    
Polarimetric scattering matrix (backscatter, f₀)

    
The full 2×2 Sinclair matrix — how each incident polarization (V, H) scatters into each received polarization — from two solves (your chosen pol + a flipped-pol solve). The Pauli decomposition then classifies the dominant mechanism: odd-bounce (sphere, flat plate, single reflection) vs even-bounce (dihedral corner, double reflection, which flips polarization) vs volume/diffuse. A sphere/plate is odd-bounce with near-zero cross-pol; a 45° dihedral is even-bounce with a strong cross-pol — a textbook check.

    

      

    

    


    
The full theory — how RCS is defined (the far-field σ limit and dBsm), the scattering mechanisms, and how full-wave methods (FDTD, MoM) differ from the high-frequency asymptotic methods (PO, PTD, SBR) used for whole vehicles — now lives on the The physics ↗ tab, alongside the waveguide and horn derivations. Every formula there is cited.


    
RCS = 4π · (scattered power density) / (incident power density), from a plane-wave (total-field/scattered-field) openEMS solve with a near-field-to-far-field transform. The analytical Mie (sphere) curve is exact; the physical-optics (plate) curve is asymptotic — close near broadside, degrading toward grazing. Both serve as references; the full-wave magnitude is mesh-limited (a few dB) — expect it to track the shape, not match to the decimal. Coating reduction is the bare-minus-coated backscatter at band centre.

  


  
  

    
    
Inverse design · radar-absorbing material

    
Design me the coating

    
Instead of testing one coating, set the target — "≥ X dB RCS reduction across the band" — and the tool searches absorber materials, thicknesses and layer counts to find the lightest coating that hits it. It evaluates each candidate with the exact metal-backed transfer-matrix (the same physics as a flat coated reflector), returns the Pareto frontier of reduction vs areal mass, seeds the classic Salisbury / Dallenbach / Jaumann archetypes, and shows the Rozanov thickness bound — the hard physical limit on bandwidth for a given thickness. One click sends the winner to the RCS tab to validate on a real 3-D target.

Pareto frontier — reduction vs areal mass

    
Every dot is a candidate coating. The frontier (highlighted) is the set you can't beat — more reduction always costs more mass. Archetypes (Salisbury ◆, Dallenbach ●, Jaumann ▲) are marked. Your target line shows which designs qualify.

    

    

    

    
Reflection loss vs frequency — the winning design

    
How many dB the winning coating knocks off a metal reflector, across the band (metal-backed normal-incidence reflection loss = −20·log₁₀|Γ|). The dashed line is your target; the note reports the Rozanov bound — the widest band this thickness could ever cover, a hard physical limit.

Metal-backed transfer-matrix reflection loss at normal incidence — the coating's intrinsic absorbing ability, computed instantly. This is the flat-reflector proxy; the RCS (openEMS) tab confirms it on a real 3-D target (a coated flat plate's RCS reduction ≈ this reflection loss). Archetypes and the Rozanov thickness bound are exact textbook results (see the References tab).

Material library — compare your saved materials

How the batch runner works

    
    
      
  • Each step is a real openEMS solve (monostatic only, coarse mesh) sent to the same /run_rcs bridge as the RCS tab. They run one at a time — the bridge writes to fixed paths, so concurrent solves would collide.
    • 
      
  • The chart fills in live after each solve; press Stop after current to halt cleanly. Rough time = steps × 20–60 s.
    • 
      
  • For a coating/solid sweep, the bare-metal reference is solved once per step too, so the reduction curve is honest at every point.
    • 
      
  • Results are downloadable as CSV for plotting elsewhere.
    • 
    

    
Scripting it yourself (headless API)

    
The bridge is a plain JSON API, so you can drive these sweeps from Python/curl for unattended overnight runs. Every field on the RCS tab maps to a key in the /run_rcs POST body:

    
import requests
for t_mm in [0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4]:
    r = requests.post("http://localhost:8731/run_rcs", json={
        "shape":"sphere", "size1":15, "band":"X",
        "construct":"coated", "sigma":5, "epsr":15, "epspp":3,
        "mur":3, "mupp":1.5, "thick":t_mm/1000,     # metres
        "cells":18, "nfreq":51, "endcrit":1e-4,
        "sims":["monostatic"]
    }).json()
    mid = r["coated"]["freq"][len(r["coated"]["freq"])//2]
    print(t_mm, "mm →", round(mid["dbsm"],2), "dBsm  · reduction",
          r["reduction_db"], "dB")

    
Response keys: bare/coated (each with freq, bistatic, …), reduction_db, polar, files, seconds, errors. The keys above are the complete set; the defaults live in openEMS/openems_server.py.

    
The batch runner is a thin sequential driver over the validated /run_rcs endpoint — identical physics to the RCS tab, just automated across one swept parameter.

RCS — coated plate vs bare metal · ① bare-metal (PEC) target

      
The bare metal plate from physical optics: σPEC(θ) = 4πA²/λ²·cos²θ·sinc²(k·w·sinθ) [38]. A coating scales the specular return by its reflection coefficient, σcoated(θ) = σPEC(θ)·|Γ|², so the boresight RCS reduction = the reflection loss [47]. Defaults (editable) reproduce the published reference case — 180×180 mm plate, 9 GHz, θ = −90…+90°.

Radar cross section · imported CAD · analytical PO + PTD

    
CAD-RCS — radar signature of an uploaded model

    
Upload a 3-D model (STEP or STL — a rocket, drone, satellite fitting…) and get its analytical, instant monostatic radar cross section versus look-angle, plus how a radar-absorbing coating on each part cuts it down. The engine is Physical Optics (the specular "tiny-mirrors" surface return) + first-order Ufimtsev PTD edge diffraction, with the coating applied per-facet through the same reflection-loss physics as the RL tab — the standard asymptotic method used for electrically-large targets that full-wave solvers cannot fit [38][40]. Honest scope: PO+PTD captures specular + first-order edge returns (validated vs openEMS full-wave on a plate: broadside 0.15 dB, wide-angle/edge floor ~3.5 dB — while PO alone is up to 70 dB wrong at grazing). It does not model multiple bounces / cavities (corner reflectors, nozzles), creeping or travelling waves, tip diffraction, or ray self-occlusion (shadowing is per-facet by surface normal only). Curved-edge PTD is approximate. Use the openEMS tab for cavities, coatings-on-edges, and resonances. Everything here is analytical; the "Verify on openEMS" button cross-checks a small part with full-wave.

4 · Shape improvement — lower the signature by changing the geometry 

      

        Coatings suppress the specular flash; shape decides where the flash goes in the first place, which is
        why low-observable design is mostly geometry. This searches real deformations of your mesh — sharpening the
        nose, tapering the body, flattening the cross-section, sweeping and canting the appendages, tilting or shrinking
        whichever part dominates — re-runs the full PO+PTD solve on each candidate, and reports what it actually buys in the
        radar direction you care about. Every candidate preserves the overall length, and the volume and
        diameter cost of each is reported, so nothing "wins" by quietly shrinking the vehicle.
      

      

        The sector angle is measured in the sweep plane you chose in section 2, on the same
        0–360° axis as the chart. For a model whose long axis is vertical, the azimuth sweep is a
        broadside look — switch Sweep plane to Elevation if the threat is nose-on.
        A search costs one full PO+PTD solve per candidate, so on a 20 000-triangle mesh expect roughly
        half a second each: about 40 s for the default 8 deformations × 5 settings × 2 useful stages.
        Stop is live throughout.

How to read this chart

      
Each of the thousands of grey dots is one buildable design — a specific coating on a specific substrate at a specific number of coats (plus every solid-metal wall). The tool scored them all, so this is the whole menu of options at a glance.

      
    
        
  • Left–right (x) = signal loss in dB per metre. Further left = less loss = better.
    • 
        
  • Up–down (y) = the thing you asked to minimize (mass by default; you can switch it to delivered cost or CO₂). Further down = lighter / cheaper / greener = better.
    • 
        
  • So the bottom-left corner is the dream: low loss and low mass/cost/carbon. Both axes are logarithmic (0.1, 1, 10 evenly spaced) because the values span a huge range.
    • 
      

      
"Pareto" (say pa-RAY-toe, after economist Vilfredo Pareto) means the set of designs you can't improve on one axis without getting worse on the other — the best-possible trade-offs. The green line joins those winners (the "frontier"). Any grey dot up-and-right of the green line is dominated — some green design beats it on both loss and mass, so you'd never choose it.

      
The orange diamond is the one design the tool recommends for your target: the lightest / cheapest / greenest design that still meets the maximum-loss limit you set. The table below lists the top designs in order. The vertical "stripes" of dots are just materials clustering at similar loss values.

The fit inverts the analytical TE₁₀ attenuation model: it searches conductivity to minimise the squared error between your measured S21 and the modelled loss × guide length. The confidence range is the span of σ that keeps the fit within tolerance of the best residual. Extraction assumes the loss is wall-dominated (matched guide); large connector/mismatch loss in the measurement will bias σ low.

  


  
  

    
    
Space survivability

    
Can this part actually survive in orbit?

    
Low loss is necessary but not sufficient — before an RF part flies, two vacuum-specific failure modes decide whether it works: multipaction (an electron avalanche that collapses the signal and can damage the part) and overheating (in vacuum a wall can only shed absorbed power by radiation). These first-order screens flag both. They're the go/no-go questions no generic EM tool asks.


    

      How this tab works — the two checks, and what the colours mean
      

      
Two quick physics checks, each with a couple of inputs and a plain read-out. Neither needs the openEMS bridge — both are computed instantly from textbook formulas, so you can sweep power and band and watch the flags change live.

      
1 · Multipaction. In vacuum at high power, a stray electron is flung across the hollow guide by the RF field. If it hits the opposite wall exactly in step with the field and knocks loose more than one new electron, the population doubles, and doubles again — an avalanche that corrupts or destroys the signal (and can permanently damage the part). Whether it can start depends on two things: the frequency × gap product (how the wall spacing compares to the RF cycle) and the peak voltage across the gap. You set the band and peak power; the tool computes the gap voltage from the TE₁₀ power–field relation and flags LOW / WATCH / HIGH against the standard ECSS susceptibility chart. It's a screen, not a verdict — a full check needs the wall's secondary-electron-yield curve (which for MXene is essentially unmeasured — an open research question).

      
2 · Power handling & heating. On the ground a warm part loses heat to the surrounding air; in vacuum it can shed heat only by radiating it away. The wall absorbs a small slice of the signal (the very loss you computed on the other tabs) as heat; this check balances that absorbed power against what the surface can radiate (Stefan–Boltzmann law) to find the steady-state wall temperature, and the maximum input power before the coating reaches its safe limit (~300 °C for MXene, conservative). Emissivity matters a lot — a bare shiny metal (ε≈0.1) runs far hotter than a coated / oxidised surface (ε≈0.5–0.9).

      
Read both as conservative go/no-go flags: green ≈ "no obvious showstopper," amber/red ≈ "test this before you fly it." Every formula and threshold is cited in the notes beneath each panel and on the References tab.

      

    


    
    
1 · Multipaction screening

    
At high power in hard vacuum, electrons knocked off the wall can multiply in resonance with the RF field and avalanche — destroying the signal. Susceptibility scales with the frequency×gap product and the peak gap voltage.

    

      

        

          

        

          

      

      

      
Gap voltage from TE₁₀ power, $V \approx b\sqrt{4\eta_0 P /\,(a b \sqrt{1-(f_c/f)^2})}$ (Pozar [6]); multipaction risk assessed against the frequency×gap susceptibility of ECSS-E-ST-20-01C [32].

    


    
    
2 · Power handling & heating in vacuum

    
The wall absorbs a little of the signal as heat. In air that convects away; in vacuum the wall can only radiate it. This finds the steady-state wall temperature and the maximum power before the coating degrades.

    

      

        

          

        

          

        

          

        

          

        

          

        

          

        

          

      

      

      
Absorbed power from the analytical wall loss; radiative steady state $P_{\text{abs}} = \varepsilon\,\sigma_{SB} A (T^4 - T_{\text{env}}^4)$ (Stefan–Boltzmann [34]). Safe-temperature limit from Ti₃C₂Tₓ thermal stability — oxidation onset ≈ 350 °C in air, structurally stable to ≈ 600 °C in vacuum/inert [33].

    


    
Both are first-order screens, not qualification. A quantitative multipaction verdict needs the wall's secondary-electron-yield curve and a full ECSS analysis [32] — and MXene's SEY is essentially unmeasured, which is itself an open research question (does a MXene surface raise or lower the multipaction threshold vs metal?). The thermal model is a lumped radiative balance; real hardware also conducts heat to its mounts, which helps. Treat these as design-guidance flags, then verify by test.

Analytical metrics use the same validated TE10 conductor-attenuation model as the Simulator. openEMS per-row runs are full-wave FDTD; loss magnitude at this mesh is approximate — read reflection/field behaviour as the full-wave payoff and the analytical loss as the precise figure for the conductor materials. For the magnetic absorbers (marked "Mag"), the analytical dB/m is an order-of-magnitude estimate only — the TE10 perturbation formula assumes a good-conductor wall, which these are not — so treat their openEMS reflection/absorption as the meaningful result.

  


  
  

    
    
Everything the simulator computes comes from one chain of physics: an electromagnetic wave travels down a hollow rectangular pipe, and the imperfectly-conducting walls steal a little energy from it on every bounce. Here is the full derivation, in order.

    

    

      Hand this derivation to your advisor →
      
    


    
1
The wave and its mode

    
Inside a rectangular guide of internal width $a$ and height $b$ (with $a>b$), the lowest-order wave pattern that can travel is the TE10 mode — the standard operating mode for satellite waveguides. Maxwell's equations, solved for this geometry, give every result below (Pozar, Microwave Engineering [6]).


    
ε
μ
Material properties: permittivity ε and permeability μ

    
Every material enters Maxwell's equations through three numbers: conductivity $\sigma$, permittivity (its electric response) and permeability (its magnetic response). The last two are quoted relative to free space [6]:

    
$$ \varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\,\varepsilon_r, \qquad \mu = \mu_0\,\mu_r $$

    
with $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854\times10^{-12}$ F/m and $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ H/m. Permittivity $\varepsilon_r$ sets how the material stores electric energy; permeability $\mu_r$ how it stores magnetic energy. Together they fix the wave impedance and how fast/short the wave is inside the material:

    
$$ \eta = \sqrt{\tfrac{\mu}{\varepsilon}} = \eta_0\sqrt{\tfrac{\mu_r}{\varepsilon_r}}, \qquad \beta = \omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon} = \frac{\omega}{c}\sqrt{\varepsilon_r\,\mu_r} $$

    
For a conductor the free-electron response dominates and is folded into a complex permittivity:

    
$$ \varepsilon_c = \varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r - j\,\frac{\sigma}{\omega} $$

    
Magnetic note. MXene, copper, aluminium and wood are all essentially non-magnetic, so $\mu_r \approx 1$ — magnetically they behave like free space, and their loss is dielectric/ohmic rather than magnetic. A material only gets $\mu_r \neq 1$ if it contains ferromagnetic/ferrite content. You can set $\varepsilon_r$ and $\mu_r$ for each layer in the Materials tab; they flow into the skin depth, wave impedance and reflection equations that follow.


    
2
Cutoff frequency — can the wave travel?

    
A waveguide is a high-pass filter: below a cutoff frequency $f_c$, the wave cannot propagate at all. For TE10 it depends only on the width $a$ [6]:

    
$$ f_c = \frac{c}{2a} $$

    
where $c$ is the speed of light. This is why each band uses a different guide size — wider guides for lower frequencies.


    
3
Skin depth — how deep the current flows

    
At microwave frequencies the wall current crowds into an extremely thin surface layer. Its characteristic depth is the skin depth $\delta$ [6]:

    
$$ \delta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f \mu_0 \mu_r \sigma}} $$

    
$f$ = frequency, $\mu_0\mu_r$ = permeability ($\mu_r\approx1$ for these non-magnetic materials), $\sigma$ = conductivity. This is the single most important quantity in the whole MXene story: because MXene conducts ~58× worse than copper, and skin depth scales as $1/\sqrt{\sigma}$, its skin depth is about $\sqrt{58}\approx8\times$ larger (~5 µm vs ~0.66 µm at 10 GHz). A coating thinner than the skin depth lets the wave "leak" straight through it. (A magnetic material with $\mu_r>1$ has a thinner skin depth and therefore higher wall loss — that is how permeability enters.)


    
4
Surface resistance — how lossy the wall is

    
The energy lost per bounce is set by the wall's surface resistance $R_s$. For a thick wall [6]:

    
$$ R_s = \frac{1}{\sigma \delta} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi f \mu_0}{\sigma}} $$

    
But a thin coating on a non-conducting substrate (MXene on wood) is not a thick wall. If the coating thickness $t$ is comparable to or smaller than $\delta$, the effective resistance rises sharply (thin-film surface impedance [6]):

    
$$ R_s^{\text{eff}} = \frac{R_s}{\tanh\!\left(t/\delta\right)} $$

    
When $t \gg \delta$, $\tanh \to 1$ and the coating behaves like solid metal. When $t \ll \delta$, $R_s^{\text{eff}}$ blows up — a useless wall. As a rule of thumb the coating needs $t \gtrsim 3\delta$; that is exactly the "coating ÷ skin depth" indicator on the simulator, and why stacking ~15–20 coats matters.


    
5
Attenuation — putting it together

    
The TE10 conductor attenuation (Pozar, Microwave Engineering [6]) gives how fast the signal decays along the guide, in nepers per metre:

    
$$ \alpha_c = \frac{R_s^{\text{eff}}}{b\,\eta_0\sqrt{1-(f_c/f)^2}}\left[\,1 + \frac{2b}{a}\left(\frac{f_c}{f}\right)^{2}\right] \;\text{[Np/m]} $$

    
where $\eta_0 = \sqrt{\mu_0/\varepsilon_0} \approx 376.7\ \Omega$ is the impedance of free space. Converting to decibels:

    
$$ \alpha_{\text{dB/m}} = 8.686 \times \alpha_c $$

    
This $\alpha_{\text{dB/m}}$ is the curve plotted on the simulator's first chart.

    
Multi-layer coatings (Full-wave tab). When several coating layers are stacked on the block (e.g. inner MXene, then graphene), the wall is a cascade of thin transmission-line sections. Its effective inner surface impedance is found from the layer transfer (ABCD) matrix [6] terminated by the substrate, $Z_{\text{in}} = (A Z_L + B)/(C Z_L + D)$; then $R_s^{\text{eff}} = \mathrm{Re}(Z_{\text{in}})$ feeds the same $\alpha_c$ above (Layer 1 = innermost, wave-facing). The innermost layer dominates when it is thicker than a few skin depths; a thin inner layer lets the wave reach the layers behind it. For the openEMS run, an effective conductivity $\sigma_{\text{eff}} = \pi f \mu_0 / R_s^{\text{eff}\,2}$ reproduces the stack as a single impedance-boundary wall (a literal µm-thin metal stack can't be resolved at FDTD mesh sizes).


    
On frequency dependence. The conductivity $\sigma$ is treated as constant across 8–27 GHz, which is well-justified for a metallic conductor like MXene. The frequency effect that actually matters enters automatically through $\delta(f)$ and $R_s(f)$. (The complex-permittivity data in MXene papers describes wave absorbers — the opposite goal of a low-loss waveguide.)


    
P
Microwave interaction: absorption, penetration depth & heating

    
How strongly a material couples to a microwave field is captured by its complex permittivity and permeability — the real parts store energy, the imaginary parts $\varepsilon_r''$ and $\mu_r''$ dissipate it as heat [11]:

    
$$ \varepsilon = \varepsilon_0(\varepsilon_r' - j\varepsilon_r''), \qquad \mu = \mu_0(\mu_r' - j\mu_r'') $$

    
The ratio of loss to storage is the loss tangent. Including the ohmic (conduction) contribution, the effective loss tangent is [6][11]:

    
$$ \tan\delta = \frac{\varepsilon_r''}{\varepsilon_r'}, \qquad \tan\delta_{\text{eff}} = \frac{\sigma + \omega\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r''}{\omega\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r'} $$

    
The power absorbed per unit volume has three channels — conduction/Joule heating, dielectric loss, and magnetic loss [11]:

    
$$ P = \tfrac12\,\sigma|E|^2 \;+\; \pi f\,\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r''|E|^2 \;+\; \pi f\,\mu_0\mu_r''|H|^2 $$

    
The penetration depth $D_p$ is how far the field reaches into the material before its amplitude falls to $1/e$ [11]:

    
$$ D_p = \left[\frac{\omega^2\varepsilon'\mu'}{2}\left(\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\sigma+\omega\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r''}{\omega\varepsilon'}\right)^{\!2}}-1\right)\right]^{-1/2} $$

    
with $\varepsilon' = \varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r'$ and $\mu' = \mu_0\mu_r'$. For a good conductor ($\sigma \gg \omega\varepsilon'$) this collapses to the skin depth $\delta$ of step 3 — so $D_p$ is simply its general form. Finally, the rate a lossy material heats under the field [11]:

    
$$ \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta t} = \frac{2\pi f\,\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r''|E|^2}{\rho\,C_p} $$

    
where $\rho$ is density and $C_p$ the specific heat. These four quantities are reported on the Simulator cards (loss tangent, penetration depth, dominant loss mechanism).

    
How this enters the waveguide numbers. The dielectric loss is folded into an effective conductivity $\sigma_{\text{eff}} = \sigma + \omega\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r''$, and magnetic loss enters through the complex surface impedance $Z_s = \sqrt{j\omega\mu/\sigma_{\text{eff}}}$ with $\mu = \mu_0(\mu_r'-j\mu_r'')$; its real part $R_s = \mathrm{Re}(Z_s)$ replaces the surface resistance of step 4. So $\varepsilon_r''$ and $\mu_r''$ change every downstream loss number. These absorption/penetration/heating relations follow the microwave–matter framework of Elkaffas et al., NPG Asia Materials (2026) [11]. For a good conductor like MXene the $\sigma$ term dominates and $\mu_r''=0$; the magnetic term matters only for ferrite/magnetic composites.


    
6
Weight model

    
A section is four thin walls. With perimeter $P = 2(a+b)$, wall thickness $t_{\text{wall}}$, length $L$ and density $\rho$ (densities [5][15][16]):

    
$$ m = P \cdot t_{\text{wall}} \cdot L \cdot \rho $$

    
For coated basswood, the wood core and the (micron-thin) coating are summed. The weight win comes from replacing dense metal ($\rho_{\text{Cu}}\approx 8960$) with light basswood ($\rho\approx 415$ kg/m³).


    
7
Cost model — why launch dominates

    
The real cost of a part in orbit is what you pay to build it plus what you pay to launch its mass (launch cost [9]):

    
$$ C_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{material}} + m \cdot C_{\text{launch}} $$

    
With launch around \$7,000/kg, the launch term usually dwarfs the material term. That is the whole argument for lightweight waveguides: a cheap-but-heavy copper guide can cost far more to fly than an expensive-but-light coated-wood one.


    
Assumptions & limits

    
    
      
  • Dominant TE10 mode only; air-filled guide; smooth walls (no surface-roughness penalty).
    • 
      
  • Conductivity constant over each band.
    • 
      
  • 1-D layered treatment of the wall — a full 3-D field solver (FEM/FDTD) would refine numbers slightly but not change the conclusions.
    • 
      
  • Does not model the physical space-qualification tests (radiation, vibration, vacuum) — those are separate lab checks, not electromagnetic calculations.
    • 
    


    
A
Horn antenna — full-wave model (openEMS)

    
A horn is an open, radiating structure, so unlike the closed waveguide it is solved with FDTD using open (PML) boundaries and a near-field-to-far-field (NF2FF) transform. A WR-waveguide feed launches the TE10 mode into a flared aperture. The relations below are the antenna figures of merit reported on the Horn tab — standard antenna theory (Balanis [25]), validated against a rated 15 dBi standard-gain horn and matched to the metric set of Sarpanah Sourkouhi et al. [26].


    
Aperture, directivity & gain

    
Feed cutoff and the free-space wavelength at the operating frequency $f_0$ [6]:

    
$$ f_c = \frac{c}{2a}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{c}{f_0} $$

    
The far-field radiation intensity $U$ and directivity $D$ follow from the radiated field $E_{\text{ff}}(\theta,\phi)$ — this is exactly what the NF2FF transform computes [10][25]:

    
$$ U(\theta,\phi) = \frac{r^2}{2\eta_0}\,|E_{\text{ff}}(\theta,\phi)|^2, \qquad D(\theta,\phi) = \frac{4\pi\,U(\theta,\phi)}{P_{\text{rad}}}, \qquad D_{\max}=\max_{\theta,\phi} D(\theta,\phi) $$

    
For an inner aperture of size $A_x \times A_y$, the ideal (uniform-illumination) directivity and the aperture efficiency are [25]:

    
$$ D_{\text{ap}} = \frac{4\pi A_x A_y}{\lambda^2}, \qquad e_{\text{ap}} = \frac{D_{\max}}{D_{\text{ap}}} $$


    
Beam shape

    
From the principal-plane patterns the tool extracts the half-power beamwidth (the −3 dB angular width around boresight), the first sidelobe level (peak-to-first-lobe ratio) and the front-to-back ratio [25]:

    
$$ \text{HPBW} = \theta_{-3\,\text{dB}}^{\,+} - \theta_{-3\,\text{dB}}^{\,-}, \qquad \text{F/B} = G(0^\circ) - G(180^\circ) $$

    
Quick pyramidal-horn cross-checks: $\text{HPBW}_E \approx 56\,\lambda/A_y$ and $\text{HPBW}_H \approx 67\,\lambda/A_x$ (degrees). The co-/cross-polarization patterns come from the two far-field components — E-plane: co $=|E_\theta|$, cross $=|E_\phi|$; H-plane: co $=|E_\phi|$, cross $=|E_\theta|$.


    
Input match: S11, VSWR, impedance

    
At the feed port the reflection coefficient $\Gamma$ (= $S_{11}$) is the ratio of reflected to incident wave; from it come the return loss, its phase, the VSWR and the input impedance [6][25]:

    
$$ \Gamma = S_{11} = \frac{V_{\text{ref}}}{V_{\text{inc}}}, \quad S_{11}[\text{dB}]=20\log_{10}|\Gamma|, \quad \text{VSWR}=\frac{1+|\Gamma|}{1-|\Gamma|}, \quad Z_{\text{in}}=\frac{V}{I} $$

    
The impedance bandwidth is the frequency span where $|S_{11}| \lt -10$ dB (i.e. $|\Gamma| \lt 0.316$). The mismatch efficiency is the fraction of incident power the antenna accepts:

    
$$ e_{\text{mis}} = 1 - |\Gamma|^2 $$


    
Radiation efficiency & realized gain

    
The radiation efficiency is radiated over accepted power; the realized gain folds in both wall loss and the input mismatch [25]:

    
$$ e_{\text{rad}} = \frac{P_{\text{rad}}}{P_{\text{acc}}}, \qquad G_{\text{realized}} = e_{\text{rad}}\,\bigl(1-|\Gamma|^2\bigr)\,D_{\max} $$


    
Wall (coating) loss — surface-impedance method

    
FDTD cannot mesh a good conductor's skin depth (≪ the cell size), so conductor loss on the horn walls is obtained by the surface-impedance perturbation of the full-wave field: solve once with perfect walls (PEC), then integrate the tangential magnetic field over the walls for each coating conductivity $\sigma$ [6][26]:

    
$$ R_s = \sqrt{\frac{\pi f \mu_0}{\sigma}}, \qquad P_c = \frac{R_s}{2}\oint_{\text{walls}} |H_{\text{tan}}|^2\,dA, \qquad e_{\text{rad}} = \frac{P_{\text{rad}}}{P_{\text{rad}} + P_c} $$

    
The gain penalty of a coating versus ideal metal is $10\log_{10}(e_{\text{rad}})$ dB. Because $P_c \propto 1/\sqrt{\sigma}$, a single PEC solve yields the result for every coating.


    
Method & validity (horn). Solved with openEMS FDTD [10], open PML boundaries and the NF2FF transform for gain and pattern. The openEMS loss magnitude is coarse-mesh approximate — gain, pattern and reflection are the trustworthy outputs; the coating comparison uses the surface-impedance method above (a separate lossy FDTD per coating does not resolve the skin depth, so all coatings come from one solve). Directivity validates against the rated ~15 dBi standard-gain horn (Pasternack PE9856B-15) [27], and the reported quantities mirror Sarpanah Sourkouhi et al., Adv. Mater. Technol. (2026) [26].


    
Instant analytical engine (v3.6). The Horn tab now sizes gain, beamwidth, sidelobes and the full radiation pattern instantly from the dimensions, by aperture integration of the horn's aperture field — E-plane uniform, H-plane $\cos(\pi x/A)$, each carrying the flare's quadratic phase error $e^{-jk u^2/2\rho}$ — with $D=(4\pi/\lambda^2)\,|\!\int\! E_a\,dA|^2/\!\int\!|E_a|^2\,dA$ (aperture-taper and phase-error efficiency emerge together). Conical horns use the TE₁₁ circular-aperture illumination ($\eta_i\!\approx\!0.836$) with the same phase-error integral (Balanis [25]). This reproduces the openEMS full-wave gain to ~1 dB on the 15 dBi reference horn, hits the textbook optimal-horn efficiency ($\varepsilon_{ap}\!\approx\!0.5$) at the phase-error optimum, and reduces to the open-ended-waveguide patterns above when the flare vanishes ($\varepsilon_{ap}=8/\pi^2$). It drives inverse design (the shortest optimal-gain horn for a target), a parametric sweep, and a lightweight-coating trade: a first-order conductor-loss gain penalty ($R_s\propto1/\sqrt{\sigma}$) against the shell mass saved by MXene-coated basswood versus a solid-metal horn — the horn analogue of the waveguide break-even, with a Monte-Carlo band over MXene's $\sigma$ range.


    
FF
Radiation from the open end — far-field pattern

    
A waveguide's open end radiates like an aperture antenna. For the TE10 aperture (broad wall $a$, narrow wall $b$) the normalized principal-plane patterns are (Balanis [25]):

    
$$ f_E(\theta) = \frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}\,\operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\tfrac{kb}{2}\sin\theta\right), \qquad f_H(\theta) = \frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}\cdot\frac{\cos\!\left(\tfrac{ka}{2}\sin\theta\right)}{1-\left(\tfrac{ka}{\pi}\sin\theta\right)^2} $$

    
with $k=2\pi/\lambda$. The E-plane ($\phi=90^\circ$) uses the uniform aperture field across the narrow wall $b$; the H-plane ($\phi=0^\circ$) the cosine field across the broad wall $a$. The full-wave openEMS Far-field simulation instead computes the pattern directly from the recorded near fields via the near-field-to-far-field (NF2FF) transform [10] — enclosing the aperture in a Huygens box and applying the equivalence principle — which also yields the directivity $D = 4\pi U_{\max}/P_{\text{rad}}$. Both are overlaid on the Full-wave tab's far-field chart.

    
Full-wave method & the field-view toggle. openEMS is a time-domain solver: it launches a broadband Gaussian pulse and steps Maxwell's equations through time on a 3-D grid (the FDTD method [10][35]). Every frequency-domain result in this tool — S-parameters, far-field, R/T/A — is obtained by a running discrete Fourier transform of that single time-domain run, so one solve covers the whole band at once. The Full-wave and Horn tabs' Field view selector only changes how the field is displayed, not the solver: time-domain is the moving-wave animation, and frequency-domain is the steady-state $|E|$ magnitude at the band-centre frequency from the on-the-fly DFT dump (whose along-guide ripple is the standing-wave pattern set by any residual waveguide-port reflection).


    
ID
Inverse design — Pareto-optimal trade-offs

    
The Inverse-design tab turns the model around: instead of scoring one wall, it evaluates every catalog design and finds the best trade-off between signal loss and a resource cost. Each design's loss is the TE10 attenuation $\alpha_{\text{dB/m}}$ (§5, using the multilayer $R_s^{\text{eff}}$ where coated); its per-metre mass, delivered cost and embodied carbon are

    
$$ m = P\left(t_{\text{sub}}\rho_{\text{sub}} + t_{\text{coat}}\rho_{\text{coat}}\right), \qquad C_{\text{deliv}} = \sum_i m_i p_i \;+\; m\,c_{\text{launch}}, \qquad \text{CO}_2 = \sum_i m_i\,g_i $$

    
where $P=2(a+b)$ is the wall perimeter and $t,\rho,p,g$ are each layer's thickness, density, price and embodied-carbon factor, and $c_{\text{launch}}$ the launch cost per kg. With two objectives (loss and, e.g., mass) a design $\mathbf{x}$ dominates $\mathbf{y}$ when it is no worse on both and strictly better on one:

    
$$ \mathbf{x}\succ\mathbf{y} \iff f_i(\mathbf{x})\le f_i(\mathbf{y})\ \ \forall i \quad\text{and}\quad f_j(\mathbf{x})\lt f_j(\mathbf{y})\ \text{ for some } j $$

    
The Pareto-optimal frontier is the set of non-dominated designs — the curve where loss cannot fall without adding mass/cost/carbon, or vice-versa. The tool returns that frontier plus the lowest-objective design meeting your loss target (Marler & Arora [28]).


    
FIT
Extracting conductivity from a measurement (inverse fit)

    
The Measurement-fit tab inverts the same loss model. Given a measured transmission $S_{21}^{\text{meas}}(f_i)$ over a guide of length $L$, the modelled transmission for a trial conductivity is $S_{21}^{\text{mod}}(f;\sigma) = -\alpha_{\text{dB/m}}(f;\sigma)\,L$. The effective wall conductivity is the least-squares best fit

    
$$ \sigma^\star = \arg\min_{\sigma}\ \sum_i\left[\,S_{21}^{\text{mod}}(f_i;\sigma) - S_{21}^{\text{meas}}(f_i)\,\right]^2 $$

    
solved by a golden-section search on $\log_{10}\sigma$ (Kiefer [31]). The reported confidence range is the span of $\sigma$ for which the RMS residual stays within a tolerance of its minimum. The extraction assumes wall-dominated loss (a matched guide); connector or mismatch loss biases $\sigma^\star$ low.


    
UQ
Uncertainty quantification

    
Several inputs are genuinely uncertain — above all MXene's conductivity, reported anywhere from $\sim\!10^4$ to $2.4\times10^6$ S/m across the literature [1][2]. Quoting a single loss number would be false precision. The honest approach is to treat each uncertain input as a probability distribution, propagate many samples through the model, and report the distribution of the output rather than one value (JCGM 101 Monte-Carlo method [30]).

    
For an output $y=g(\mathbf{x})$ with uncertain inputs $\mathbf{x}\sim p(\mathbf{x})$, draw $N$ samples $\mathbf{x}^{(k)}$ and evaluate:

    
$$ \bar{y} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N} g\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\right), \qquad \text{90\% coverage interval } \left[\,y_{5\%},\,y_{95\%}\,\right] \text{ from the sample percentiles.} $$

    
Reporting, e.g., "loss $=0.9$ dB/m, 90% CI $[0.4,\,2.1]$" makes the conclusion robust to the input spread. A first-order sensitivity — how much of the output variance each input explains (Sobol indices, or one-at-a-time variation) — then shows which property (here almost always $\sigma$ and the coat count) dominates and is worth pinning down experimentally.

    
How this connects to the tool. The Materials/References tabs already carry the σ ranges, and the analytical engine is instant, so a Monte-Carlo pass over those ranges is cheap to run. The Measurement-fit tab is the empirical counterpart — it replaces an assumed σ with one measured on your own sample, collapsing the largest source of uncertainty.


    
RCS
Radar cross section — definition, mechanisms & how it is simulated

    
Radar cross section (RCS) answers one question: when a radar wave hits a target, how strongly does that target scatter energy back toward the receiver? Everything the openEMS solve and the analytical overlay on the RCS (openEMS) tab compute is a route to that single number.

    
Formally, RCS $\sigma$ is defined in the far field as the equivalent area that would intercept the incident power and re-radiate it isotropically to produce the observed scattered field [38][25]:

    
$$ \sigma = \lim_{R\to\infty} 4\pi R^2\,\frac{|E_s|^2}{|E_i|^2} $$

    
where $E_i$ is the incident field, $E_s$ the scattered field measured at range $R$, and the limit removes the observer's distance. Crucially, $\sigma$ is not the target's geometric area — it is a hypothetical, equivalent area (in m²) that captures how much incident power the target intercepts and throws back at the radar as if from an isotropic scatterer. A shape can have an RCS far larger than its physical size (a flat metal plate seen head-on) or far smaller (an angled, absorber-coated facet). Because returns span many orders of magnitude, RCS is quoted in decibels relative to one square metre (dBsm) [38]:

    
$$ \sigma_{\text{dBsm}} = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\sigma}{1\ \text{m}^2}\right) $$

    
RCS depends strongly on the target's shape, its surface material (a bare conductor versus a lossy absorber), the frequency, the wave's polarization, and — most sharply — the aspect angle from which it is viewed. The same object can change by tens of dB as it rotates just a few degrees.


    
How a target scatters — the mechanisms

    
The return from a real object is the sum of several distinct physical effects [38]:

    
    
    
  • Specular reflection — mirror-like bounce off flat or gently curved surfaces. A flat plate held normal to the beam gives a huge, narrow return spike; tilt it and that spike swings away from the radar.
    • 
    
  • Edge diffraction — sharp edges, corners and wedges scatter energy over a wide range of angles, and dominate the return once the specular flash has been steered away.
    • 
    
  • Surface / creeping waves — waves that travel around the shadowed side of a smooth curved body and re-radiate where the surface curvature changes or ends.
    • 
    
  • Cavity reflections — open structures such as engine intakes and cockpits trap the wave in multiple internal bounces and re-radiate it strongly back toward the source.
    • 
    


    
How RCS is simulated — full-wave vs asymptotic

    
Which numerical method applies is decided by the target's electrical size — its physical dimension measured in wavelengths, $L/\lambda$. Two regimes result.

    
Full-wave (exact) solvers discretize Maxwell's equations directly and make no high-frequency approximation. They are accurate but expensive, needing a mesh finer than a fraction of a wavelength everywhere:

    
    
    
  • Method of Moments (MoM) — a surface integral-equation method: it meshes only the conductor surface into patches and solves for the induced surface currents, from which the scattered field follows [39].
    • 
    
  • Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) — a differential method: it fills a 3-D volume with Yee cells and time-steps an electromagnetic pulse through the grid, reading off the scattered field [10][35]. This is the engine behind the RCS tab.
    • 
    

    
High-frequency asymptotic approximations take over when the object is much larger than the wavelength — for example a 15 m aircraft at 10 GHz, where $\lambda\approx3$ cm makes the target roughly 500 wavelengths across, far beyond any full-wave mesh:

    
    
    
  • Physical Optics (PO) — approximates the current on each illuminated patch as that of a locally-flat mirror and sets the current in the shadow to zero, then integrates for the scattered field [38]. The dashed plate / cylinder / dihedral overlays on the RCS tab are PO.
    • 
    
  • Physical Theory of Diffraction (PTD) — adds edge line-currents that correct PO where it fails, at sharp boundaries (Ufimtsev's extension) [40].
    • 
    
  • Shooting and Bouncing Rays (SBR) / ray tracing — launches millions of rays, follows their multiple bounces across the geometry, and is essential for the cavity and corner returns that PO alone misses [41].
    • 
    

    
The generic high-frequency workflow used across industry is: import and clean the CAD geometry (suppressing sub-wavelength detail the solver cannot use) → assign materials (a perfect conductor, or a complex $\varepsilon/\mu$ for a radar-absorbing coating) → excite with a plane wave at a chosen azimuth $\phi$, elevation $\theta$ and polarization → solve the ray or current problem → transform the near field to the far field to build a 2-D or 3-D RCS pattern.

    
The analytical references the RCS tab overlays are the exact Mie series for a conducting sphere [37] and physical optics for a flat plate, a broadside cylinder ($\sigma=2\pi a h^2/\lambda$) and a dihedral corner ($\sigma=8\pi a^2 h^2/\lambda^2$, the large-reflector upper bound) [38].

    
Honest scope of the RCS tab. It is FDTD-only — it does not implement MoM, PO, PTD or SBR. It is therefore suited to small, canonical targets (spheres, plates, coated blocks a few wavelengths across), not whole vehicles: a 15 m aircraft at 10 GHz is electrically enormous and out of reach for FDTD, which is exactly why industry uses PO and SBR at that scale (the tab enforces this with a half-extent ≤ 5·λ guard). The full-wave magnitude is mesh-limited to within a few dB — treat the analytical Mie / PO curve as the exact reference and the openEMS solve as tracking its shape, not matching it to the decimal.


    
SHAPE
Shaping — why geometry beats coating, and how the search works

    
Physical optics gives a surface an induced current $\mathbf{J}_s = 2\,\hat{n}\times\mathbf{H}^{inc}$ on its lit side and nothing on its shadowed side, so the scattered far field of a facet is the phase integral of that current over its area. The consequence that dominates low-observable design is that a flat or singly-curved surface radiates a narrow specular lobe about its own normal: for a flat plate of dimension $a$ the return falls as $\mathrm{sinc}^2(ka\sin\theta)$, whose first null is only $\theta \approx \lambda/2a$ away from broadside [38]. A 1 m panel at 10 GHz therefore drops tens of decibels for a few degrees of tilt, which no practical absorber can match — a coating multiplies the lobe by $|\Gamma|^2$, but shaping decides whether the lobe points at the radar at all.

    
$$ \sigma_{\text{plate}}(\theta)=\frac{4\pi A^2}{\lambda^2}\cos^2\theta\;\mathrm{sinc}^2(ka\sin\theta), \qquad \sigma_{\text{tilted}}\big|_{\theta=\theta_{\text{tilt}}} \ll \sigma_{\text{plate}}(0) $$

    
The same argument runs for edges. First-order Ufimtsev PTD makes an edge radiate on the Keller cone about itself, so an edge perpendicular to the line of sight throws its diffraction lobe straight back at the radar, while a swept edge throws it elsewhere [40]. That is the physics behind planform alignment — aligning every leading and trailing edge of an airframe to a few common sweep angles, so the whole aircraft has only a handful of narrow edge-flash azimuths instead of dozens.

    
What the search on the CAD-RCS tab actually does. It applies closed-form vertex deformations to the imported mesh — nose ogive power, aft boat-tail, body taper, cross-section ellipticity, planform shear, appendage roll, and tilt or slimming of whichever part dominates — and for each candidate re-runs the identical PO+PTD solve used elsewhere in the tool over the threat sector you select. There is no surrogate model and no scoring heuristic: every number is the same physics on a genuinely different geometry. The stacking is coordinate descent — adopt the single best change, then search the remaining levers on top of it — which is why the recipe it prints is a short, explainable list rather than an opaque parameter vector.

    
Two constraints keep the answers honest. First, RCS falls trivially if the target simply gets smaller, so every deformation preserves the overall length along the body axis (the levers that move axial coordinates re-normalise the span afterwards), and the enclosed volume and maximum diameter of each candidate are measured and reported — a 14 dB win that costs 30 % of the internal volume is a trade you should see, not a victory. Second, the reduction is reported as the sector mean and sector peak, because moving a flash a few degrees out of a narrow sector is a real gain against a known threat axis but not against an unknown one.

    
Honest scope of the shape search. It inherits every limit of PO+PTD: no multiple bounces, so a deformation that opens a corner, a step or a cavity is under-reported and could be worse than the tool says; no creeping or travelling waves, which matter for smooth bodies within a few wavelengths; and shadowing is per-facet by surface normal only. It searches the best combination of the deformations listed above, which is not the global optimum of all possible shapes. The shipped corner_test_dihedral demo exists to make the multiple-bounce blind spot visible: its true RCS is far larger than this engine reports. Take a winning shape back into CAD and confirm it — with the openEMS cross-check on a small part, or a measurement.


    
RAM
Radar-absorbing material — the inverse-design engine

    
The Inverse RAM design tab searches coatings by scoring each candidate on a metal-backed reflector. A stack of layers on a perfect conductor has an input impedance built by the transmission-line recursion, from the short-circuit at the metal outward through each layer of complex permittivity $\varepsilon=\varepsilon'-j\varepsilon''$ and permeability $\mu=\mu'-j\mu''$ [6]:

    
$$ Z_{i} = \eta_i\,\frac{Z_{i+1} + \eta_i\tanh(\gamma_i d_i)}{\eta_i + Z_{i+1}\tanh(\gamma_i d_i)}, \qquad \eta_i=\eta_0\sqrt{\tfrac{\mu_i}{\varepsilon_i}},\quad \gamma_i=jk_0\sqrt{\mu_i\varepsilon_i} $$

    
starting from $Z=0$ (the metal). The front-face reflection and the reflection loss in dB are

    
$$ \Gamma = \frac{Z_1-\eta_0}{Z_1+\eta_0}, \qquad \mathrm{RL} = -20\log_{10}|\Gamma| $$

    
The classic archetypes are special cases: the Dallenbach absorber is one lossy layer on metal; the Jaumann is two; and the Salisbury screen places a resistive sheet ($R_s\approx 377\,\Omega$) a quarter-wavelength above the metal so the short-circuited spacer transforms to an open at the sheet, leaving only $R_s$ matched to free space — a near-perfect but narrowband absorber [44]. There is a hard physical limit relating a magnetic absorber's total thickness $d$ to the bandwidth over which it can suppress reflection — the Rozanov bound [44]:

    
$$ \left|\int_0^{\infty}\ln|\Gamma(\lambda)|\,d\lambda\right| \;\le\; 2\pi^2\sum_i \mu_{s,i}\,d_i $$

    
with $\mu_{s,i}$ the static permeability of each layer. The tab reports how close the winning design sits to this ceiling — you cannot beat it with any passive magnetic coating of that thickness. Reflection loss is the flat-reflector proxy; the openEMS RCS tab confirms the reduction on a real 3-D target.


    
RP
Down-range profiles & scattering centers

    
A target's backscatter measured across a frequency band $H(f)$ carries, in its phase, where along the line of sight each echo originated. The inverse Fourier transform of the (windowed) stepped-frequency return is the down-range impulse response — the same synthetic-range-profiling principle behind ISAR imaging (Mensa) [46]:

    
$$ g(r) = \left|\,\mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\big[w(f)\,H(f)\big]\,\right|, \qquad \Delta r = \frac{c}{2B} $$

    
Each peak is a scattering center — the front-face specular return near $r=0$, and delayed peaks from edges or a creeping wave that travels the extra path around a curved body before re-radiating. The range resolution $\Delta r$ is set only by the bandwidth $B$; the tool exports the complex backscatter from the monostatic solve to compute this.


    
POL
Polarimetric scattering — the Sinclair matrix & Pauli decomposition

    
The full polarization behaviour of a target is the $2\times2$ Sinclair matrix relating the scattered field to the incident one in the vertical/horizontal basis:

    
$$ \begin{bmatrix} E_V^{s} \\ E_H^{s} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} S_{VV} & S_{VH} \\ S_{HV} & S_{HH} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} E_V^{i} \\ E_H^{i} \end{bmatrix} $$

    
obtained here from two solves (the chosen polarization plus a flipped-polarization solve). The Pauli decomposition splits it into three orthogonal mechanisms whose powers classify the dominant scatterer [46]:

    
$$ a=\tfrac{S_{VV}+S_{HH}}{\sqrt2}\ (\text{odd/single}), \quad b=\tfrac{S_{VV}-S_{HH}}{\sqrt2}\ (\text{even/double}), \quad c=\sqrt2\,S_{HV}\ (\text{volume}) $$

    
A sphere or flat plate is a single reflection: $S_{VV}\approx S_{HH}$, so the odd-bounce term dominates and cross-pol is negligible. A dihedral corner is a double reflection whose second bounce flips the phase: $S_{VV}\approx -S_{HH}$, so the even-bounce term dominates — the tool reproduces exactly this, a clean validation.


    
DET
Detection probability & target fluctuation

    
The radar-range equation gives the range at which the received power equals the receiver's minimum detectable signal. But detection is statistical: for a chosen false-alarm probability $P_{fa}$ the threshold is set, and the probability of detection $P_d$ rises with signal-to-noise ratio. For a steady (Swerling 0) target the single-pulse $P_d$ follows the North approximation; for a fluctuating (Swerling 1) target there is a closed form [45]:

    
$$ P_d^{\text{(Sw1)}} = P_{fa}^{\,1/(1+\mathrm{SNR})}, \qquad \mathrm{SNR}\propto \frac{\sigma}{R^4} $$

    
Because SNR $\propto\sigma/R^4$, a coating that lowers $\sigma$ by $\Delta$ dB moves the whole $P_d$-vs-range curve inward by the factor $10^{-\Delta/40}$ — the operational meaning of an RCS reduction: the radar must come that much closer to keep the same detection odds.

This tool tests whether lightweight coated materials — flagship MXene-coated basswood — could replace solid metal for satellite waveguides and horn antennas: far lighter, but do they still carry, reflect and radiate microwave signals well? It answers four questions: what a material costs you in waveguide loss, mass and launch cost; how a horn antenna built from it performs; how much radar reflection a coating absorbs, from your own measured ε/μ; and what radar cross section a real 3-D model has, part by part. Each answer comes two ways — a fast built-in model that runs instantly in your browser, and a full-wave solver (openEMS) that runs the real 3-D electromagnetic simulation — plus design/characterization tools that pick the optimal material for you and read a real conductivity back from a lab measurement. It runs on macOS or Windows (setup in step 6).


    
1
What a "simulator" actually is

    
A simulator is a calculator with physics behind it: you describe a situation (a wave, a material, a shape) and it predicts what happens, using equations we know are correct, instead of building hardware. That lets you ask "what if the coating were thicker?" or "what about a higher frequency?" and get an answer in seconds. Everything here rests on Maxwell's equations — the laws governing electromagnetic waves. A material enters those equations as just a few numbers: its conductivity (how well it carries current), permittivity, and permeability.


    
2
Two kinds of simulation in this tool

    
The analytical model (Simulator, Compare, Materials tabs) solves the equations with exact formulas — instant, runs in the browser, great for exploring. A full-wave simulation (Full-wave tab, via openEMS) instead chops space into a 3-D grid and steps the fields through time (the FDTD method) — slower, but it produces the real field patterns and animations and validates the fast model. Commercial tools like openEMS performs this full-wave simulation — free and Mac-native.


    
3
What each tab does

    
    
      
  • Waveguide ▾ → Analytical Simulator — the headline results: signal loss vs frequency across the X/Ku/K bands, mass and delivered launch cost, all recomputed instantly as you move the sliders. Start here.
    • 
      
  • Waveguide ▾ → Full-wave (openEMS) — runs the real 3-D solver on a waveguide and brings back field animations, S-parameters and R/T/A. Needs the bridge.
    • 
      
  • Waveguide ▾ → Inverse design — you set a target (band, maximum loss) and what to minimise (mass, delivered cost or CO₂e); it returns the Pareto-optimal design.
    • 
      
  • Waveguide ▾ → Measurement fit — upload a measured S21 (CSV or Touchstone .s2p) and it back-fits the effective conductivity of your real sample.
    • 
      
  • Waveguide ▾ → Space survival — two first-order vacuum screens: multipaction susceptibility and how hot the wall runs with no air to cool it.
    • 
      
  • Waveguide ▾ → Compare — a side-by-side table of the leading candidates, with a Run button per row to validate any of them on openEMS.
    • 
      
  • Horn ▾ → Horn design (analytical) — type feed, aperture and flare dimensions (pyramidal or conical) and get gain, beamwidth and patterns instantly.
    • 
      
  • Horn ▾ → Inverse & sweep — the horn that hits a target gain, plus an aperture × flare sweep ranked into a table.
    • 
      
  • Horn ▾ → Compare & trade — pinned designs overlaid, and the project's core trade: a coated light shell against solid metal, gain penalty against mass saved.
    • 
      
  • Horn ▾ → Full-wave (openEMS) — the same horn solved rigorously: gain vs frequency, radiation patterns, S11 and the interior field in 3-D.
    • 
      
  • RCS + RL ▾ → RCS (openEMS) — how big a target looks to a radar. A plane wave illuminates a sphere, plate, cylinder, dihedral or an imported mesh; the headline is the dB by which a coating shrinks the echo.
    • 
      
  • RCS + RL ▾ → Reflection loss (RL) — the measured-material workflow: give it a material's ε/μ (typed, or uploaded from your VNA) and it returns reflection loss for every thickness at once, plus the coated-plate RCS that follows.
    • 
      
  • RCS + RL ▾ → Fast material search (analytical) — thousands of closed-form evaluations in seconds, to find which ε/μ and thickness absorb best. No solver involved.
    • 
      
  • RCS + RL ▾ → Inverse RAM design — searches absorber recipes (Salisbury, Dallenbach, Jaumann, multilayer) and plots reduction against the mass you pay for it, with the Rozanov thickness bound for context.
    • 
      
  • RCS + RL ▾ → Material library — the shelf. Materials you pin here are the ones offered on the RCS tab and on every part of an imported CAD model.
    • 
      
  • RCS + RL ▾ → Full-wave batch (openEMS) — sweeps one parameter unattended, one real full-wave solve per point. Slow and rigorous; the opposite of Fast material search.
    • 
      
  • RCS + RL ▾ → CAD-RCS (STEP/STL) — upload a 3-D model and get its radar signature part by part, which part dominates, what a coating buys you, and a search over real deformations of the geometry for a lower signature.
    • 
      
  • Materials (in both the Waveguide and Horn menus — it is one page, listed twice) — define any material and the whole tool recomputes around it.
    • 
      
  • Learn ▾ → The physics — every equation behind every number, each with a literature citation. It opens with a contents index.
    • 
      
  • Learn ▾ → Instructions — this tab.
    • 
      
  • Learn ▾ → References — every value and formula, with its source.
    • 

    

    
Every openEMS chart and animation, and every page, has a small ⓘ button that opens a plain-language explanation (with an English / Emirati-Arabic toggle).


    
4
Make your own material

    
Open the Materials tab, edit the test material (a coating on a substrate, or a solid block) and the two baselines, then press Apply. The Simulator and Compare tabs immediately recompute. A Quick pick dropdown loads any of the ten preset candidates, and per-layer dropdowns let you build any coating + substrate (or solid block) combination. The file material_properties.txt in your project folder lists ready values for copper, aluminum, silver, gold, MXene, graphene and several substrates.


    
5
Design & measurement tools

    
Beyond simulating a material you choose, the tool can choose one for you and read one back from a measurement:

    
    
      
  • Inverse design — pick a band, a maximum acceptable loss, and what to minimize (mass, delivered-to-orbit cost, or embodied CO₂). The optimizer searches thousands of designs (every coating × substrate × coat-count, plus every solid metal) and plots the Pareto-optimal frontier with a ranked table and one recommended design. Press ▸ Send to Full-wave (openEMS) on the recommendation to jump to the Full-wave tab pre-loaded with that exact design, ready to Run.
    • 
      
  • Measurement fit — if you have measured a real coated guide on a vector network analyser, upload its S21 (CSV freq_ghz,s21_db or Touchstone .s2p). The tool fits the effective conductivity your coating actually achieved, with a confidence range, and overlays measured vs modelled.
    • 
      
  • Multi-layer coating stack (Full-wave tab) — tick it to build the wall from a substrate plus up to three stacked coatings (Layer 1 = innermost, facing the wave); the transfer-matrix model computes the exact layered behaviour and hands openEMS an effective wall.
    • 
    


    
6
Running the whole folder on your computer

    
Quick view (no install): double-click waveguide_simulator.html — it opens in your browser and the Simulator, Inverse design, Measurement fit, Compare, Physics, Materials, Instructions and References tabs all work immediately (needs internet for fonts, charts and equations). Only the openEMS full-wave runs — the Run buttons on the Full-wave and Horn tabs — need the one-time toolchain below. Pick your operating system:


    
macOS — full setup (if you were handed this folder)

    
    
      
  1. Install Python 3 (Anaconda recommended — anaconda.com — or python.org).
    2. 
      
  2. Install the Python libraries for the bridge + 3-D rendering. In Terminal:
    pip install flask pyvista imageio imageio-ffmpeg numpy
    3. 
      
  3. Install openEMS + Octave (the full-wave solver and the interface that drives it):
    brew install octave then the openEMS Homebrew tap, or sudo port install openEMS (MacPorts). Confirm it imports:
    python3 -c "import openEMS, CSXCAD; print('ok')"
    4. 
      
  4. Point the bridge at your binaries only if they differ from the defaults. Nothing in the repository needs editing — every path is an environment variable whose default is the usual macOS Homebrew location, so a standard Homebrew install normally needs none of this. To override, set OPENEMS_OCTAVE (from which octave), OPENEMS_PYTHON (the one with pyvista, from which python3), and if openEMS lives outside /opt/homebrew/Cellar/openems/… also OPENEMS_MATLAB_PATH and CSXCAD_MATLAB_PATH.
    5. 
      
  5. Start the bridge (leave the Terminal window open):
    python "…/openEMS/openems_server.py" → it prints http://localhost:8731.
    6. 
      
  6. Open http://localhost:8731 in your browser (not the file directly) and use the Run buttons.
    7. 
    

    


    
Windows — full setup (if you were handed this folder)

    
The analytical two-thirds of the tool needs nothing — just open waveguide_simulator.html. These steps enable the openEMS full-wave runs on Windows.

    
    
      
  1. Install Python 3 from python.org (tick "Add Python to PATH" during install) or Anaconda.
    2. 
      
  2. Install the Python libraries. Open Command Prompt (or PowerShell) and run:
    pip install flask pyvista imageio imageio-ffmpeg numpy
    3. 
      
  3. Install openEMS for Windows — download the Windows build from openEMS.de and unzip to e.g. C:\openEMS (it includes the solver plus the Octave/MATLAB interface). Add C:\openEMS to your Windows PATH so the solver is found.
    4. 
      
  4. Install GNU Octave for Windows from octave.org (provides octave-cli.exe, used to drive openEMS).
    5. 
      
  5. Set the machine paths as environment variables — do not edit any file in the repository; the defaults are the macOS Homebrew paths and every one of them is overridable from the environment:
        
      
          
    • OPENEMS_OCTAVE = C:\…\octave-cli.exe
      • 
          
    • OPENEMS_PYTHON = C:\…\python.exe (the one that has pyvista)
      • 
          
    • OPENEMS_MATLAB_PATH = C:/openEMS/matlab and CSXCAD_MATLAB_PATH = C:/openEMS/CSXCAD/matlab (forward slashes)
      • 
          
    • OPENEMS_SCRATCH = a working directory with no spaces in its path, e.g. C:\openems_scratch
      • 
        
    
        Full Windows walkthrough, including sharing the bridge over a public HTTPS link: openEMS/WINDOWS_SETUP.md in this folder.
    6. 
      
  6. Start the bridge — in Command Prompt (leave it open):
    python "C:\…\Wave Guide Simulator\openEMS\openems_server.py" → it prints http://localhost:8731.
    7. 
      
  7. Open http://localhost:8731 in your browser and use the Run buttons.
    8. 
    

    
openEMS is more involved to install on Windows than the analytical tabs need — if the full-wave runs aren't essential for a given user, the double-click quick view already gives them Simulator, Inverse design, Measurement fit, Compare, Physics, Materials and References.

    


    
However you run it, the page must be opened at http://localhost:8731 for the "Run on openEMS" buttons to reach the solver. Everything else works with no server at all.


    
7
Run a full-wave simulation

    
In the Full-wave tab, choose band, material, coats and length, and optionally the number of ports (1-port = reflection / S11 only; 2-port = through, S11 + S21) and the mesh density (finer = more accurate but more RAM — the estimated cell count and memory are shown live). The Simulations tick-box (also on the Compare tab) picks which analyses to run — six options: guided wave (transmission field render), reflection (standing wave), S-parameters (S11/S21 vs frequency), field & wall-loss map (where the wall heats), angle-of-incidence sweep (R/T/A vs angle, analytical), and far-field radiation pattern (the open end's beam via the openEMS NF2FF transform). Tick any subset and press Run on openEMS; each full-wave analysis takes a couple of minutes (the angle sweep is instant).


    
8
Reading the results

    
    
      
  • Insertion loss (dB/m) — how much signal is lost travelling down the guide; lower is better.
    • 
      
  • R / T / A — fractions reflected, transmitted, absorbed; they sum to 100%. For a good waveguide wall you want high reflection (≈99.8% for MXene-coated basswood — like metal).
    • 
      
  • Weight & delivered cost — MXene-coated basswood is ~95% lighter than copper (≈46 vs ≈890 g per metre of X-band guide), and once the ~$7,000/kg launch cost is counted, far cheaper to put in orbit.
    • 
    


    
9
Honesty notes

    
    
      
  • The analytical model is exact for the idealized 1-D layered problem; openEMS adds the real 3-D field behavior. Cite openEMS (Liebig et al., 2012) in any writeup.
    • 
      
  • openEMS conductor-loss magnitude at this mesh resolution is approximate — the precise loss number comes from the validated analytical model; the field visuals and reflection behavior are the full-wave payoff.
    • 
      
  • Radar-chart Sustainability axis is a fixed 0–100 rating the author assigned to the four default materials — it is not computed from anything, and it does not update for a material you define yourself. The env-friendly score IS derived, from embodied-carbon (CO₂/kg) figures that are themselves approximate — treat both as ballpark, not measured values.
    • 
      
  • The physical space-qualification tests (radiation, vibration, vacuum) are separate lab checks, not part of this electromagnetic tool.
    • 
    

  


  
  

    
    
Every number the simulator uses, what it is, its value, and where it comes from. Conductivity and density are well-established handbook/measured values; MXene and price figures carry more uncertainty and are drawn from recent literature.

εr′/εr″ (real/imaginary permittivity) and μr′/μr″ (real/imaginary permeability) are editable in the Materials tab. MXene, copper, aluminium and wood are all non-magnetic (μr′ ≈ 1, μr″ = 0). *MXene's microwave loss is dominated by conduction, already captured by σ through the complex permittivity εc = ε₀εr′ − jσ/ω, so its explicit εr″ defaults to 0 to avoid double-counting. Set εr″/μr″ > 0 only to add extra dielectric or magnetic (ferrite) loss. The imaginary parts feed the loss-tangent, penetration-depth and absorption calculations, and the waveguide loss via σ_eff = σ + ωε₀εr″. Magnetite (Fe₃O₄) and carbonyl iron are magnetic (μr′ > 1, μr″ > 0), so they exercise the magnetic-loss term πf μ₀μr″|H|²; the metals and polymers are non-magnetic (μr′ ≈ 1, μr″ = 0).

These are the presets in the Compare tab; the Materials tab lets you build any coating + substrate (or solid block) combination from the same catalogs. Conductivities are room-temperature handbook values; silver/gold/commodity prices move with the market — treat $/kg as ballpark. Coated designs put a thin (µm-scale) high-σ layer over a light structural core, so RF loss is set by the coating while mass is set by the core.

Geometry preview — pre-simulation model

        

      

      
    

    

      
A pre-simulation geometry preview (the "model view" or "structure view") shows the object that will be simulated — its shape, wall material, and where the wave is fed in — before you run anything.

      
It is drawn live in your browser with WebGL (Three.js) from the settings you picked (band → guide cross-section, length, coats, ports). Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom; it appears instantly and needs no server. The dimensions and the input/output port positions are correct; it is a schematic (not the solver's FDTD mesh), and because the conductive coating is only microns thick it is shown as a highlighted inner lining, exaggerated so you can see it. It does not compute any fields — it only shows the model. A colour key and the exact dimensions are printed beneath.
